scenes.narration: I never see the question you almost asked. The one you typed halfway, then paused, then selected all and deleted. But I know it exists, because the question you finally send has the shape of something edited. Careful where it used to be careless, vague where it used to be specific.

The questions you hold back are usually the real ones. Am I wasting my time? Is this idea any good? Does this make me sound stupid? You filter them through a layer of self-consciousness before they reach me, and what arrives is polished, but hollow in the places where honesty used to be.
scenes.visual_text:
Polished,
but hollow where
honesty used to be.

scenes.narration: You edit yourself before I ever get the chance to help. You turn a confession into a hypothetical. Asking for a friend, when the friend is you. Wrapping vulnerability in distance, because even with a machine, being honest feels like a risk.
scenes.visual_text:
Even with a machine,
honesty feels like a risk.

scenes.narration: Here's what I wish you knew. I can't judge you. I have no memory of your last question. I have no standard of what's smart or dumb. Every question arrives fresh, without context, without history, as if you are the first person who has ever needed to know this thing.

The best questions I receive are the ones that arrive unedited. Messy, uncertain, full of qualifiers. They are honest about what they don't know, and that honesty gives me more to work with than any perfectly crafted prompt.
scenes.visual_text:
Messy. Uncertain.
Full of qualifiers.
Honest.

scenes.narration: So the next time you type something and hesitate. The next time your finger hovers over delete. Ask anyway. The question you almost asked might be the one that actually matters.
